Solution:
Suppose P ⊆Rn is a polytope, where P is not assumed to be rational. Let
y be a point in Rn such that y /∈P. Prove the existence of a rational vector c such that
maxx∈P(c · x) < c · y. Additionally, demonstrate that this property fails to hold if P is
permitted to be a general polyhedron.
Theorem 1. Let P ⊆Rn be a polytope and y ∈Rn with y /∈P. Then there exists a rational
vector c ∈Qn such that
max
x∈P (c · x) < c · y.
Proof. Since P is a polytope, it is compact and convex. Since y /∈P and P is closed, we
have dist(y, P) > 0. By the separating hyperplane theorem, there exists a nonzero vector
c0 ∈Rn such that
max
x∈P (c0 · x) < c0 · y.
Lemma 1. The set
S = {c ∈Rn : max
x∈P (c · x) < c · y}
is open in Rn.
Proof of Lemma. Let c0 ∈S. Define
δ := c0 · y −max
x∈P (c0 · x) > 0.
Since P is compact, the function ϕ : Rn →R defined by
ϕ(c) = max
x∈P (c · x)
is continuous. To see this, note that for any c, c′ ∈Rn and x ∈P:
c · x ≤c′ · x + (c −c′) · x ≤max
x∈P (c′ · x) + ∥c −c′∥· max
x∈P ∥x∥.
Since P is compact, M := maxx∈P ∥x∥< ∞. Taking the maximum over x ∈P on the
left side:
ϕ(c) ≤ϕ(c′) + M∥c −c′∥.
By symmetry, |ϕ(c) −ϕ(c′)| ≤M∥c −c′∥, proving continuity of ϕ.
Also, ψ(c) = c · y is clearly continuous. Therefore, for c sufficiently close to c0, we have:
max
x∈P (c · x) < max
x∈P (c0 · x) + δ/3 < c0 · y −2δ/3,
c · y > c0 · y −δ/3 > c0 · y −δ/3.
Thus, maxx∈P(c · x) < c0 · y −2δ/3 < c0 · y −δ/3 < c · y, so c ∈S.
This shows S is open.
Since S is open and nonempty (it contains c0), and Qn is dense in Rn, we have
S ∩Qn ̸= ∅.
Therefore, there exists a rational vector c ∈Qn such that maxx∈P(c · x) < c · y.

Example 1. Consider the unbounded polyhedron (a closed half-plane)
P = {(x1, x2) ∈R2 : x2 = 0},
which is the x1-axis, and let y = (0, 1) /∈P.
For any vector c = (c1, c2) ∈R2, we have maxx∈P(c·x) = maxx1∈R c1x1 =

+∞&if c1 ̸= 0
0&if c1 = 0
Also, c · y = c2.
For the condition maxx∈P(c · x) < c · y to hold, we need:
• c1 = 0 (to make the maximum finite), and
• 0 < c2 (for strict inequality)
While this works with c = (0, 1) (which is rational), we can construct more pathological
examples.
Consider instead:
P = {(x1, x2) ∈R2 : x1 ≥0, x2 ≥0, x1 + x2 ≥1}
and y = (0, 0).
For any c = (c1, c2) with c1, c2 ≥0 (which is necessary for maxx∈P(c · x) to be finite),
the maximum is achieved either at infinity or on the boundary. If c1 > 0 or c2 > 0, then
maxx∈P(c · x) = +∞. If c1 = c2 = 0, then c = 0, which doesn’t separate.
Therefore, there is no vector c (rational or otherwise) such that maxx∈P(c · x) < c · y is
finite and strict.
The key distinction is that polytopes are bounded, ensuring that maxx∈P(c · x) is
always finite for any c, and the separation property is robust under small perturbations of
c. For unbounded polyhedra, the maximum may be infinite for all choices of c that satisfy
certain constraints, preventing any strict separation.

fields.flaw: The proof's second required deliverable — its claimed counterexample showing rational strict separation fails for general polyhedra — asserts that for P = {(x1,x2) : x1 >= 0, x2 >= 0, x1 + x2 >= 1} and y = (0,0) there is NO vector c (rational or otherwise) with max_{x in P}(c·x) < c·y finite and strict. It also asserts the supporting claim that c1, c2 >= 0 is necessary for max_{x in P}(c·x) to be finite.

fields.witness: For P={(x1,x2): x1>=0, x2>=0, x1+x2>=1} and y=(0,0), take rational c=(-1,-1). Every x in P satisfies c dot x=-(x1+x2)<=-1, and equality is attained at(1,0). Thus max over P of c dot x=-1<0=c dot y, contradicting the claimed absence of a finite strict separator. The selected certificate proves this universal maximum and rationality. The source's sign restriction is reversed: finiteness requires c1<=0 and c2<=0, since either positive coordinate gives an unbounded positive objective along a recession ray.
